buildUp: To survive the pressure at depth, the crew have to live inside a thick steel cylinder with domed ends, which is the strongest shape for its weight against an even squeeze from all sides.
To dive and surface, the boat needs a way to change its weight, so ballast tanks sit outside the pressure hull, flooded through vents and blown dry with air stored at a couple of hundred bar.
A diesel engine needs air, so it can only run on the surface or while breathing through a snorkel mast; it charges big lead-acid batteries that power the boat underwater.
An electric motor driving a large, slow seven-bladed propeller gives the quietest possible push, because spinning slowly avoids the bubbles and hum a fast propeller makes.
Because the sea blocks light and radio, the boat needs sonar arrays to listen and retractable masts in the sail for periscopes, radio and the snorkel when near the surface.
A smooth outer casing covered in sound-absorbing tiles wraps it all, and planes at the bow, sail and stern steer it up, down and sideways like the fins of a fish.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Make the boat's weight adjustable so it can match the weight of the water it displaces exactly, and then hover like a fish. Ballast tanks take on seawater to dive and are blown out with compressed air to surface, while a thick round steel hull keeps the sea out. Underwater it runs on stored battery power, because there's no air for a diesel and an electric motor makes almost no noise.

hardParts.title: A hull that holds back the ocean
hardParts.why: The pressure hull has to resist hundreds of tonnes per square metre, yet every hole through it, for torpedo tubes, masts, hatches and the propeller shaft, is a weak spot. Small departures from a perfect circle can let it buckle at a lower depth than designed, so the steel is rolled and welded with extreme care and the welds are inspected exhaustively.

hardParts.title: Being quieter than the sea around you
hardParts.why: Every pump, gear and propeller blade makes sound that travels for kilometres underwater. Machinery is mounted on rubber mounts, the propeller is big and slow to avoid cavitation, the bubbles that pop noisily when water pressure drops behind a blade, and the casing is tiled to swallow sonar pings. A single rattle can undo all of it.

hardParts.title: Coming back up, every time
hardParts.why: If the boat floods a compartment or loses power deep down, it has to be able to rise on its own. An emergency blow sends high-pressure air into the ballast tanks to empty them in about a minute, giving the boat spare buoyancy of about 10 to 15 percent, and the system has to work even when everything else has failed.

principles.explanation: A submarine dives by taking on seawater until it weighs exactly as much as the water it pushes aside, so it neither rises nor sinks. Any object in water is pushed up with a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside, which is Archimedes' principle. A ship floats because it's lighter than the water its hull displaces; a submarine lets about 200 tonnes of seawater into its ballast tanks to reach that balance. Then small trims of water and the angle of its planes hold it at a chosen depth. The balance is delicate: the hull squeezes slightly as it goes deeper, so it loses a little buoyancy and must be trimmed constantly.
principles.title: Floating is a weighing contest

principles.explanation: Every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere of pressure, so at 300 m the sea pushes on the hull with about 30 atmospheres, roughly 300 tonnes on every square metre. A cylinder is the efficient shape to resist this because the load spreads evenly around it as squeezing, not bending. For a round hull, the stress in the steel is roughly the pressure times the radius divided by the thickness, so a 6 m hull a few centimetres thick sees a couple of hundred million pascals: within the strength of special high-strength steels, but not ordinary ones.
principles.title: Ten metres, one atmosphere

principles.explanation: Seawater soaks up radio and light but carries sound for tens of kilometres, so a submarine sees by listening, and its own noise is what most often gives it away. Seawater is salty and conducts electricity, so it soaks up radio waves within a few metres, and even sunlight fades to darkness within a couple of hundred metres. Sound, by contrast, travels at about 1,500 m/s in water. That's why it listens with sonar and has to put up a mast to use radio.
principles.title: The sea carries sound, not light or radio

principles.explanation: Because the power needed to push a hull through water rises roughly with the cube of speed, a submarine on battery power creeps most of the time and sprints only when it must. Going five times faster needs over a hundred times the power. That's why the same batteries can drive the boat at about 4 knots for a few days but at about 20 knots for only an hour or so.
principles.title: Drag rises steeply with speed

firstPrinciples.problem: Build a ship that can disappear under the sea for days, choose any depth it likes, and come back up again, with a crew of about 35 breathing normal air inside. The deeper it goes the harder the water squeezes, the further it is from the air its engines need, and the more its own noise could give it away to someone listening. It must be heavy enough to sink, light enough to rise, and quiet enough to hide.

questions.answer: Salty seawater conducts electricity and absorbs radio waves within a few metres. To use radio it must come near the surface and raise a mast above the waves.
questions.question: Why can't a submarine talk to its base by radio while it's deep underwater?

questions.answer: A diesel burns fuel with oxygen from the air, and there's no air underwater. It can only run them on the surface or through a snorkel, so underwater it lives off the batteries the diesels charged.
questions.question: Why doesn't the submarine run its diesel engines underwater?

questions.answer: A fast-spinning blade lowers the water pressure behind it so much that bubbles form and collapse, making noise and damage. A big, slow propeller moves the same water more gently, avoiding those bubbles and staying quiet.
questions.question: Why is the propeller so large, and why does it turn so slowly?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The submarine wins by hiding, not by fighting, and that's what makes the diesel-electric design so effective. With the diesels off, the only sound is a slow electric motor and a big propeller turning at no more than about 200 rpm, so a battery-powered boat can be quieter than the ocean around it. Its weakness, needing to come up and snort air to recharge, is the price paid for that silence.

name: Diesel-Electric Submarine
overview:
A submarine is a ship that can sink on purpose and come back up. It does this with ballast tanks between its two hulls: opening vents lets seawater flood in so it gets heavier and dives, and blowing compressed air into the tanks pushes the water out so it rises. Once submerged, small trims of water and the angle of its planes keep it hovering at any depth, like a fish.

The crew live and work inside the pressure hull, a thick steel cylinder that keeps out the crushing weight of the sea; every 10 m of depth adds another atmosphere of pressure. Around it, the outer casing gives a smooth, quiet shape and is covered in rubbery tiles that soak up sonar pings.

This boat is diesel-electric. On or near the surface it runs diesel generators, breathing through a snorkel mast, to charge huge banks of batteries. Deep underwater it shuts the diesels off and runs on battery power alone: an electric motor turns a large, slow propeller, which makes it one of the quietest machines in the ocean. It hunts by listening with sonar arrays in the bow and attacks with torpedoes fired from tubes at the front.

parts.description: Streamlined free-flooding nose that houses the sonar array and the muzzles of the torpedo tubes.

details.didYouKnow: Early submarines had sharp, ship-like bows for running on the surface; once boats spent most of their time submerged, designers switched to the rounded whale-like nose because it is quieter and faster underwater.
details.howItWorks: The bow is not watertight: it fills with sea as the boat dives, so it never has to resist depth pressure, only give the boat a smooth rounded nose. Behind its skin sit the bow sonar, the forward main ballast tank and the front ends of the six torpedo tubes, whose muzzles open through small shutter doors that close flush to keep the flow quiet. Its blunt, rounded shape suits a boat that spends most of its life underwater rather than ploughing through waves.
keyNumbers: Six torpedo muzzles about 0.5 m across
Floods fully within seconds of diving
details.madeOf: Mild or high-strength steel plating for the structure, with panels of glass-reinforced plastic in front of the sonar. GRP lets sound pass through almost unchanged while staying tough and corrosion-free.

parts.name: Bow section

parts.description: Light outer skin over the middle of the boat, covered in rubbery anechoic tiles that absorb sonar.

details.didYouKnow: Anechoic tiles can occasionally come loose at sea, and photos of boats returning to port sometimes show gaps like missing teeth where tiles have been lost.
details.howItWorks: The casing is a thin fairing wrapped around the top and sides of the pressure hull, giving a flat deck to walk on when surfaced and a smooth shape underwater. The gap between it and the pressure hull is free-flooding and holds pipes, mooring gear, the flank sonar arrays and the compressed-air bottles outside the crew's living space. Its anechoic tiles soak up incoming sonar pings and also damp the hum of machinery leaking out from inside.
keyNumbers: Tiles typically a few cm thick
Thousands of tiles cover the boat
Plating only a few mm to about 1 cm thick
details.madeOf: Fairly thin steel plate or glass-reinforced plastic panels, with tiles of specially formulated rubber or polyurethane glued on. The tiles contain tiny voids that turn sound energy into a little heat.

parts.name: Outer casing half

parts.description: Tapering tail cone that smooths the flow of water into the propeller.

details.didYouKnow: The teardrop hull with a single propeller at a pointed tail came out of research in the 1950s and is still the basic shape of most submarines, because it is so efficient and quiet underwater.
details.howItWorks: The stern cone narrows the hull smoothly so water flowing along the sides closes in gently on the propeller instead of tumbling off a blunt edge. Getting this flow even all the way round matters, because uneven flow makes each blade feel a pulsing load, which shows up as noise on enemy sonar. The X-form planes are mounted on the cone, and the propeller shaft runs out through its tip to the hub.
keyNumbers: Narrows from about 6.6 m to under 1 m
Overall hull about 10 times as long as it is wide
details.madeOf: Steel plating shaped over internal frames, faired and coated like the rest of the casing. Much of it is free-flooding, so it only needs to be stiff, not pressure-proof.

parts.name: Stern section

parts.description: Tall fin on top that holds the masts and periscopes and gives the bridge a lookout spot when surfaced.

details.didYouKnow: Some navies call this the sail and others the fin; both names replaced the older term conning tower, which on early boats was a real watertight room.
details.howItWorks: The sail is a streamlined fin that sheathes the masts and periscopes when they are lowered, so they slide up and down inside it without sticking out into the flow. When surfaced, the crew climb up a trunk to a small open bridge at the top, which is the only high lookout point on a boat that otherwise sits barely above the waves. It sits above the control room so the optical periscope can pass straight down into it.
keyNumbers: Roughly 4 to 5 m tall above the casing
Holds four or so retractable masts
details.madeOf: Steel or glass-reinforced plastic plating over a steel frame, free-flooding inside. The sail is not part of the pressure hull, so it can be built light.

parts.name: Sail (fin)

parts.description: Small wings on the sail that steer the boat up or down near the surface and at periscope depth.

details.didYouKnow: Some deep-ocean submarines can turn their sail planes vertical so the sail can push up through sea ice without snapping them off.
details.howItWorks: Each plane is a small hydrofoil that the crew tilt from the control room; angling it makes water push the front of the boat up or down. Mounting them high on the sail keeps them away from the bow sonar, so the swirling water they create does not drown out what the sonar is listening to. They are especially useful at periscope depth, where the boat must hold its height within a metre or so while waves try to push it around.
keyNumbers: Swing typically up to about 25 degrees
Depth held within about 1 m at periscope depth
details.madeOf: High-strength steel spars covered in shaped plating, turned by hydraulic actuators inside the sail. They need to be stiff enough not to flutter at speed.

parts.name: Sail planes

parts.description: One of four rudder-planes set in an X; together they steer and control depth, and still work if one jams.

details.didYouKnow: X-form sterns were first tried on an experimental teardrop-hulled submarine in the 1960s, but they only caught on widely once computers could blend the four fin movements automatically.
details.howItWorks: Instead of a cross of separate rudders and hydroplanes, four identical fins stick out diagonally from the tail. A computer moves all four together in different combinations, so that the same fins steer left and right and pitch the boat up and down. Because every fin contributes to both jobs, a single jammed fin can be balanced by the other three, and the diagonal layout keeps the fins within the hull's width for berthing and sitting on the seabed.
keyNumbers: Set at about 45 degrees to the vertical
details.madeOf: High-strength steel structure with smooth plating, each fin driven by its own hydraulic actuator. Separate actuators are what give the redundancy.

parts.name: X-form stern plane

parts.description: Retractable planes near the bow that tilt the nose up or down; they fold away when surfaced.

details.didYouKnow: Planes work like an aircraft's wings but underwater, and because water is about 800 times denser than air, a fin the size of a door can push hard enough to steer a boat of nearly 2,000 tonnes.
details.howItWorks: These small hydrofoils sit low on the bow and act on the front of the boat, the opposite end from the stern planes. Tilting them changes the boat's angle and depth together, giving fine control at slow speed when the stern planes have little bite. When the boat surfaces or comes alongside, they rotate and fold flat against the hull so waves and harbour walls cannot damage them.
keyNumbers: Fold away in well under a minute
Most effective at a few knots
details.madeOf: Steel spars and plating on a pivoting shaft that passes into the hull through a watertight seal, worked by hydraulics. Folding gear adds weight, so the planes are kept compact.

parts.name: Bow diving planes

parts.description: Raised, free-flooding casing along the top of the boat: a flat place to stand when surfaced, with slots that let water in and out when diving.

details.didYouKnow: The slots can sing like a bottle when water rushes past them, so designers shape them and sometimes fit shutters to stop a submarine giving itself away.
details.howItWorks: The flat raised casing gives the crew somewhere to stand when the boat is on the surface, and it hides mooring gear, air bottles and pipework out of the flow. It is not watertight at all: rows of slots along its sides let water pour in as the boat dives and drain away as it surfaces, so the thin plating never has to resist depth pressure. Bollards and cleats fold down or sit in pockets, because anything sticking out would make noise underwater.
keyNumbers: Stands well under a metre above the pressure hull
Runs most of the boat's length
Flood slots are usually tapered and shuttered to keep the flow quiet
details.madeOf: Thin steel or glass-fibre panels on light frames, removable for access and covered in the same rubbery tiles as the rest of the outer skin. Being free-flooding, it can be built far lighter than the pressure hull under it.

parts.name: Deck casing

parts.description: Thick high-strength steel cylinder that keeps the sea out; the crew and machinery live inside it.

details.didYouKnow: Designers usually build in a margin so the hull would only collapse at roughly one and a half times its test depth, the deepest the boat routinely goes.
details.howItWorks: The pressure hull is a long cylinder stiffened by steel ring frames every metre or so, which stop the shell from buckling inwards. At depth, the sea squeezes it evenly from all sides and the hull actually shrinks slightly, which the crew can hear as creaks. Everything that must stay dry and at normal air pressure lives inside, and every hole through it, from hatches to pipes, is a carefully designed weak point.
keyNumbers: Steel typically a few cm thick
Test depth typically a few hundred metres
About 30 atmospheres of sea pressure at 300 m
details.madeOf: Special high-yield steel, made tough enough to bend slightly rather than crack, and welded under strict control. Each weld is X-rayed or ultrasonically checked, because one flaw could start a failure.

parts.name: Pressure hull half

parts.description: Domed end cap closing the pressure hull; domes spread the sea's push evenly, like an egg.

details.didYouKnow: For the same thickness, a hemisphere is about twice as strong as a cylinder against outside pressure, which is why the ends of pressure vessels are domed rather than flat.
details.howItWorks: The forward dome closes off the front of the pressure hull and sees the full sea pressure head-on. A dome carries load as pure compression spread evenly in every direction, which is far more efficient than a flat wall. This one is also pierced by the rear ends of the six torpedo tubes, so their breech doors open into the torpedo room just inside it, and each penetration is heavily reinforced.
details.madeOf: The same high-yield steel as the hull, pressed or spun into a curved shape and welded to the cylinder. Thicker rings are added around each torpedo tube opening.

parts.name: Pressure hull end dome (forward)

parts.description: Tank between the hulls that floods with seawater to dive and is blown out with compressed air to surface.

details.didYouKnow: Main ballast tanks are either fully flooded or fully empty in normal use; the fine balancing at depth is done with much smaller trim tanks inside the pressure hull.
details.howItWorks: The forward tank wraps around the front of the pressure hull with open flood holes at the bottom and vent valves at the top. Opening the vents lets air escape so the sea rushes in from below and the boat loses its spare buoyancy; to surface, the vents shut and compressed air is blown in, pushing the water back out through the holes. Being at the bow, it also controls whether the nose goes down first when diving.
keyNumbers: Vents open to dive in about a minute
Front edge about 20 m forward of the boat's centre
details.madeOf: Steel plating that only has to withstand small pressure differences, because the tank is open to the sea at the bottom. It is coated heavily against corrosion since it is often wet.

parts.name: Main ballast tank (forward)

parts.description: Domed end cap closing the pressure hull; domes spread the sea's push evenly, like an egg.

details.didYouKnow: Stern glands are designed to let a tiny trickle of seawater through to lubricate and cool the seal; it is pumped away from a small drain well inside the boat.
details.howItWorks: The aft dome seals the back of the pressure hull just behind the propulsion motor. Its key feature is the opening for the propeller shaft, which turns continuously through a stern gland that has to stop seawater getting in while letting the shaft spin and slide slightly as the hull squeezes. The thrust of the propeller is fed into the hull structure just inside it through a thrust bearing.
keyNumbers: Faces the same sea pressure as the forward dome
details.madeOf: High-yield steel matching the hull, with a thick machined boss around the shaft opening to carry the gland and spread the loads.

parts.name: Pressure hull end dome (aft)

parts.description: Tank between the hulls that floods with seawater to dive and is blown out with compressed air to surface.

details.didYouKnow: A single-hull boat like this one has much less spare buoyancy on the surface than a double-hulled design, so it floats low, with waves often washing over the casing.
details.howItWorks: The aft tank does the same job as the forward one at the other end of the boat, so together they lift or sink the hull evenly. Divers can flood the two tanks a moment apart to put a gentle bow-down angle on as the boat leaves the surface. When surfacing in a hurry, both are blown hard together so the boat rises level rather than shooting up nose-first.
keyNumbers: Together the tanks give about 10 to 15 percent spare buoyancy
Sits about 20 m aft of centre
details.madeOf: Steel plating with flood openings at the bottom and vent valves at the top, shaped to follow the narrowing stern. Like the forward tank it needs good paint to resist constant wetting.

parts.name: Main ballast tank (aft)

parts.description: Steel wall dividing the pressure hull into compartments, so one flooded section doesn't sink the boat.

details.didYouKnow: Many small diesel-electric boats have only two or three compartments, so each bulkhead protects a large share of the crew; escape hatches are usually placed so each end of the boat has one.
details.howItWorks: This aft bulkhead separates the living and battery spaces from the engine room, where the diesels and the propulsion motor run. It keeps engine noise, heat and any fire or flooding in the machinery space from spreading forward. A watertight door lets crew pass through, and it is shut whenever the boat goes to action stations or something goes wrong.
keyNumbers: Door typically roughly 0.7 to 0.8 m wide
Dozens of sealed cable and pipe glands
details.madeOf: Welded steel plate, often slightly dished or heavily stiffened, with a circular door and many sealed fittings for cables and pipes passing through.

parts.name: Watertight bulkhead 1

parts.description: Steel wall dividing the pressure hull into compartments, so one flooded section doesn't sink the boat.

details.didYouKnow: Watertight doors on submarines are usually round or oval because curves have no corners where stress concentrates, so they can be lighter for the same strength.
details.howItWorks: This forward bulkhead sits roughly beneath the sail, dividing the torpedo room and control area from the accommodation behind. If the bow section flooded, for example from a damaged torpedo tube, closing its door would keep the rest of the boat dry. It also gives a firm anchor for the weapon handling gear and forward equipment.
keyNumbers: Roughly 7 m forward of the boat's centre
Door typically roughly 0.7 to 0.8 m wide
details.madeOf: Welded steel plate stiffened with ribs, with a circular watertight door and sealed penetrations. Being near the heavy torpedo stowage, it is built stoutly.

parts.name: Watertight bulkhead 2

parts.description: Banks of high-pressure air used to blow the ballast tanks and surface in an emergency.

details.didYouKnow: As compressed air rushes out of the bottles it cools sharply, which is why valves in blow systems can ice up and why designers fit filters and keep the air very dry.
details.howItWorks: Compressors on board squeeze ordinary air into these steel bottles, which are stored outside the pressure hull. When the boat needs to surface, valves release this air into the main ballast tanks, where it expands and pushes the seawater out. In an emergency blow, the crew release a large amount at once so the boat rises fast even if it is heavy with flooding.
keyNumbers: Several thousand litres of bottle volume in total
An emergency blow can empty the tanks in about a minute
details.madeOf: Thick seamless steel cylinders, forged or drawn from solid billets so there are no welds to fail at very high pressure.

parts.name: Compressed-air bottles

parts.description: Cylinder of hundreds of underwater microphones that listens for ships and submarines miles away.

details.didYouKnow: Sound travels about 1,500 m per second in seawater, more than four times faster than in air, and it bends with temperature layers, so sonar operators study the water itself as much as the targets.
details.howItWorks: Rows of hydrophones arranged around a cylinder each pick up sound slightly earlier or later depending on its direction. Computers combine these tiny delays to form listening beams pointing in many directions at once, building a picture of noises all around the bow. It mostly listens passively, since sending a ping would give the boat away, but it can transmit if needed.
keyNumbers: Can detect noisy ships tens of km away
details.madeOf: Piezoelectric ceramic elements, which make a voltage when squeezed by sound, set in rubber or plastic mountings and housed behind an acoustically transparent window.

parts.name: Bow sonar array

parts.description: Steel tube with a watertight door at each end; water or air pressure pushes the torpedo out.

details.didYouKnow: The 533 mm tube size dates back more than a century and is still used by many navies today, so torpedoes are almost always built to fit it.
details.howItWorks: A torpedo is loaded from inside through the rear door, then the tube is flooded and pressure-equalised with the sea before the bow cap opens. A burst of water or air pushes the weapon out, or in some designs the torpedo simply swims out under its own power. An interlock stops both doors ever being open at once, because that would flood the torpedo room.
keyNumbers: Reloading takes typically several minutes per tube
details.madeOf: Thick steel tube machined smooth inside, with heavy hinged doors at each end and an internal guide rail. The tube is part of the pressure boundary, so it is built to hull standards.

parts.name: Torpedo tube

parts.description: Wire-guided torpedo about 6 m long that steers itself to the target with its own sonar.

details.didYouKnow: Modern heavyweight torpedoes are designed to explode beneath a ship rather than hit it, so the bubble from the blast lifts and then drops the hull, breaking its back.
details.howItWorks: Once launched, the torpedo pays out a thin wire from spools on both itself and the boat, so the submarine can steer it using its own better sonar. As it closes in, the torpedo's sonar in its nose takes over, either listening or pinging to home in. An electric motor or a heat engine spins its contra-rotating propellers or pump-jet.
details.madeOf: Aluminium or steel body sections, with the warhead at the front, electronics and batteries or fuel in the middle, and the motor at the back.

parts.name: Heavyweight torpedo

parts.description: Long strip of hydrophones along each side for passive listening at low frequencies.

details.didYouKnow: Low-frequency sound can travel hundreds of kilometres in the deep sound channel, a layer of the ocean where temperature and pressure bend sound back towards the middle.
details.howItWorks: These long strips of hydrophones listen along each side of the boat, where the hull is quietest and away from the bow's flow noise. Because the array is long, it can pick up the deep, low-frequency hum of distant engines and propellers, which travels much further underwater than high-pitched sound. Comparing when a sound reaches different parts of the array also helps estimate how far away its source is.
keyNumbers: Tuned to low frequencies, often below about 1 kHz
details.madeOf: Piezoelectric sensors in flat panels of polyurethane or rubber, fixed to the casing over sound-isolating mountings so the boat's own vibration does not reach them.

parts.name: Flank sonar array

parts.description: Slim optical periscope raised just above the waves to take a quick look while staying hidden.

details.didYouKnow: Low power is usually about 1.5x rather than 1x because the image seen down a long tube looks smaller than life, and 1.5x makes things appear their natural size.
details.howItWorks: A series of prisms and lenses carries the image down a long tube to an eyepiece in the control room, where the officer walks it round to scan the horizon. The head is very slim to leave only a tiny wake and to be hard to see. It is raised for only a few seconds at a time, just high enough to clear the waves, then lowered again.
keyNumbers: Low and high power, often about 1.5x and 6x
Exposed for typically a few seconds
details.madeOf: A stainless or high-strength steel tube that must resist bending in the flow, with precision optical glass inside, often filled with dry nitrogen to stop fogging.

parts.name: Attack periscope

parts.description: Camera mast with daylight and thermal sensors that feeds pictures to screens in the control room.

details.didYouKnow: Because optronic masts do not need to pass through the hull, newer designs have moved the control room away from directly under the sail to wherever it fits best.
details.howItWorks: Instead of a long optical tube, this mast carries cameras in its head: a daylight camera, a thermal imager and often a laser rangefinder. It can take a full 360 degree panorama in a second or two, then lower, letting the crew study the recording on screens without keeping the mast up. Only cables pass through the hull, so the mast does not need to reach down into the control room.
keyNumbers: Full sweep in roughly a second or two
Thermal camera sees warm ships at night
details.madeOf: A steel or composite mast with a sealed sensor head, often shaped and coated to reduce radar reflections.

parts.name: Optronic mast

parts.description: Air pipe raised above the surface so the diesels can breathe while the boat stays submerged.

details.didYouKnow: The snorkel was developed in the Netherlands in the 1930s and widely adopted in the Second World War; sailors still call snorkelling snorting, from the German word Schnorchel.
details.howItWorks: Raised just above the waves at periscope depth, the snorkel draws fresh air down to the diesels while a separate pipe carries the exhaust out, usually below the surface. A float or sensor valve at the top slams shut when a wave washes over it, so the sea cannot get in. The diesels then briefly suck air from inside the boat, causing a sharp pressure drop the crew feel in their ears.
keyNumbers: Snorkel at about 10 to 15 m keel depth
Typically a few hours a day of snorting
details.madeOf: Steel induction pipe with a head valve, often with a radar-absorbing coating. The exhaust mast must tolerate hot, corrosive gases.

parts.name: Snorkel mast

parts.description: Antenna mast for communications and for detecting enemy radar.

details.didYouKnow: Radar has to travel out and back to see you, while ESM only needs the outgoing pulse, so a well-tuned receiver can hear a radar from several times further away than the radar can detect the boat.
details.howItWorks: This mast is raised at periscope depth so its antennas clear the water, letting the boat send and receive radio and satellite messages. The ESM sensors on it listen for radar pulses, telling the crew if an aircraft or ship is searching nearby. ESM works passively and usually detects a radar long before that radar can see the mast.
keyNumbers: Covers frequencies from HF radio up to many GHz
Raised for minutes rather than hours
details.madeOf: A steel mast with antennas in a glass-fibre radome, which lets radio waves through while keeping the sea out.

parts.name: Radio & ESM mast

parts.description: The nerve centre under the sail, with the steering, diving, sonar and weapons consoles.

details.didYouKnow: Control rooms used red lighting at night so that the officer's eyes stayed adapted to the dark before looking through the periscope.
details.howItWorks: From here the crew steer the boat, hold its depth, manage the ballast and trim, and run the sonar and weapons consoles. One or two operators at the ship-control station handle the rudder and planes, often helped by an autopilot. The commanding officer brings all this together, deciding when to raise masts, when to snort and when to attack.
details.madeOf: Steel consoles on shock-mounted frames, with flat screens and controls; cabinets are bolted to the deck so they survive the jolt of a nearby explosion.

parts.name: Control room

parts.description: Stacked bunks, a galley and mess where about 35 crew live for weeks at a time.

details.didYouKnow: Submarine food is famously good, partly to keep morale high in a crowded steel tube with no daylight for weeks.
details.howItWorks: This compartment packs sleeping, eating and washing into a space smaller than many flats. Bunks are stacked three high with curtains, and on some patrols junior sailors share a bunk in shifts, known as hot bunking. The galley cooks for the whole crew round the clock, and fresh water is made from seawater with distillers or reverse osmosis.
details.madeOf: Light aluminium and plastic fittings with fire-resistant fabrics, all chosen to save weight and space and to give off little toxic smoke in a fire.

parts.name: Crew quarters

parts.description: Hundreds of large lead-acid cells under the deck that power everything when submerged.

details.didYouKnow: If seawater floods a battery compartment it can react with the acid to produce chlorine gas, which is one reason batteries are sealed beneath the deck.
details.howItWorks: Each lead-acid cell gives about 2 volts, so hundreds are wired in series to reach the high voltages that run the propulsion motor. The forward bank sits low in the hull under the crew spaces, where its great weight helps keep the boat stable. While charging it gives off hydrogen, so powerful ventilation and catalytic burners keep that gas from building up.
keyNumbers: Each cell roughly half a tonne
Typically a couple of hundred cells in this bank
details.madeOf: Lead plates in dilute sulphuric acid inside tough plastic cases. Lead-acid is heavy but cheap, robust and well understood.

parts.name: Forward battery bank

parts.description: Second battery bank; together they give a few days of slow, silent running.

details.didYouKnow: Batteries make up a large share of a diesel-electric boat's weight, so they double as ballast low in the hull, keeping the boat upright.
details.howItWorks: The aft bank sits just behind the forward one and is wired with it so the boat can draw on both, or isolate one if it is damaged. Together they store enough energy for about a few days at slow speed, but only an hour or so near top speed, because drag rises steeply with speed. The captain always balances the need to move fast against draining the batteries and having to snort.
keyNumbers: Roughly 4 knots for a few days
Up to about 20 knots for an hour or so
details.madeOf: Large lead-acid cells like the forward bank, packed tightly with cable runs and cooling between them.

parts.name: Aft battery bank

parts.description: Diesel engine coupled to a generator that recharges the batteries while snorkelling.

details.didYouKnow: Early submarines used petrol engines, but the fumes caused explosions, so diesels, whose fuel is much less volatile, took over in the early 1900s.
details.howItWorks: The forward diesel generator runs when the boat is surfaced or snorting, turning a generator that recharges the batteries and powers the boat. It sits on a raft of shock mounts that soak up vibration so the hull does not ring. The two generators can run together for a fast charge, or one alone if the other is down for maintenance.
details.madeOf: A cast-iron or alloy engine block with steel crankshaft and pistons, coupled to a generator of copper windings in a steel frame.

parts.name: Diesel generator 1

parts.description: Diesel engine coupled to a generator that recharges the batteries while snorkelling.

details.didYouKnow: The fraction of time a submarine must spend snorting to keep its batteries charged is called the indiscretion rate, and lowering it is a key goal of modern designs.
details.howItWorks: The aft diesel generator is the twin of the first and sits a few metres behind it, closer to the propulsion motor. Running both at once roughly halves the time spent snorting, which is when the boat is most likely to be detected. Its exhaust and air pipes run up through the hull to the snorkel mast.
details.madeOf: Like its twin, a cast block with forged steel moving parts, plus a generator, mounted on resilient isolators.

parts.name: Diesel generator 2

parts.description: Large, slow-turning electric motor that drives the propeller shaft directly, with no gearbox to make noise.

details.didYouKnow: Electric motors are so quiet that at slow speeds a diesel-electric submarine on batteries can be quieter than many nuclear submarines, which have to keep their reactor pumps running.
details.howItWorks: This large electric motor turns the propeller shaft directly at the same slow speed as the propeller, so there is no gearbox. Avoiding gears removes a big source of whine that sonar could hear. It takes power from the batteries, or from the diesels while snorting, and its speed is controlled electronically.
details.madeOf: Copper windings and steel laminations, often with permanent magnets in the rotor for high efficiency. The frame is built to be very stiff and is shock-mounted.

parts.name: Propulsion motor

parts.description: Steel shaft from the motor out through a sealed gland in the hull to the propeller.

details.didYouKnow: Shafts are balanced and aligned very precisely, because even a slight wobble makes a regular thump that sonar operators can recognise.
details.howItWorks: The shaft carries the motor's twisting force aft and the propeller's push forward. A thrust bearing inside the hull passes that push into the hull structure, which is what actually drives the boat. Where it leaves the pressure hull, it passes through a stern gland and is supported further aft by water-lubricated bearings, so it never needs oil out in the sea.
details.madeOf: Forged high-strength steel, often sleeved with corrosion-resistant metal where it runs in seawater.

parts.name: Propeller shaft

parts.description: Bronze boss the blades are fixed to.

details.didYouKnow: When submarines are in dry dock, their propellers are often covered in tarpaulins, because the exact blade shape is a closely guarded secret.
details.howItWorks: The hub is the solid centre of the propeller that fits on a tapered end of the shaft and is held on by a large nut. The blades are cast as one piece with it or bolted on, and the hub must carry their full thrust and twisting load into the shaft. A smooth, rounded cap covers the nut so water flows cleanly off the back of the propeller instead of swirling into a noisy vortex.
details.madeOf: Nickel-aluminium bronze, which resists seawater corrosion and is tough and easy to cast in large pieces.

parts.name: Propeller hub

parts.description: One of seven curved, skewed blades shaped to turn slowly without making bubbles that sonar could hear.

details.didYouKnow: Deeper water presses harder on the blades and stops bubbles forming, so a submarine can usually go faster quietly when it is deeper.
details.howItWorks: Each blade is curved back like a scimitar, so different parts of it meet uneven water from the hull at slightly different times, smoothing out pulses of noise. The large size lets the propeller turn slowly while still pushing plenty of water. Turning slowly keeps the pressure on the blades from dropping so low that the water boils into bubbles, called cavitation.
keyNumbers: Turns at up to about 200 rpm
details.madeOf: Nickel-aluminium bronze, cast and then carefully ground and polished to an exact shape.

parts.name: Propeller blade

summary: A 65 m patrol submarine with a crew of about 35: diesel generators charge large batteries that drive a single electric motor and propeller, so it can run almost silently underwater for days.
